title: III. Ilusha’s Funeral. The Speech At The Stone
paragraphs: He really was late. They had waited for him, and had already decided to carry the pretty little flower-decked coffin to the church without him. It was the coffin of poor little Ilusha. He had died two days after Mitya was sentenced. At the gate of the house, Alyosha was met by the shouts of the boys, Ilusha's schoolmates. They'd all been waiting for him impatiently and were glad he'd finally come. There were about twelve of them, all with their satchels or school-bags slung over their shoulders. “Father will cry — stay with father,” Ilusha had told them as he lay dying, and the boys had remembered. Kolya Krassotkin was in front of them all.

“I'm so glad you've come, Karamazov!” he cried, holding out his hand to Alyosha. “It's awful here. Really horrible to see. Snegiryov isn't drunk — we know for a fact he hasn't touched a drop today — but he looks as though he were.... I'm always the manly type, but this is awful. Karamazov, if I'm not holding you up, one question before we go in?”
“What is it, Kolya?” said Alyosha.
“Is your brother innocent, or guilty? Was it him who killed your father, or the valet? Whatever you say, that's how it'll be for me. I haven't slept the last four nights, thinking about it.”
“The valet killed him. My brother is innocent,” Alyosha answered.
“That's exactly what I said!” cried Smurov.
“So he'll die an innocent victim!” Kolya exclaimed. “Though he's ruined, he's happy! I could almost envy him!”
“What do you mean? How can you say that? Why?” Alyosha cried, surprised.
“Oh, if only I, too, could sacrifice myself someday for the truth!” said Kolya, with enthusiasm.
“But not in a cause like that — not with such disgrace, such horror!” said Alyosha.
“Of course.... I'd like to die for all humanity, and as for disgrace, that doesn't matter to me — our names can perish. I respect your brother!”
“So do I!” the boy who had once declared he knew who founded Troy cried out, suddenly and unexpectedly, blushing to the tips of his ears, red as a peony, just as he had that other time.

Alyosha went into the room. Ilusha lay with his hands folded, his eyes closed, in a blue coffin trimmed with a white frill. His thin face had barely changed, and strangely enough, there was no smell of decay from the body. His expression was serious, almost thoughtful. His hands, folded across his chest, looked especially beautiful, as though carved from marble. There were flowers in his hands, and the coffin, inside and out, was decked with flowers, sent early that morning by Lise Hohlakov. But there were flowers from Katerina Ivanovna too, and when Alyosha opened the door, the captain had a bunch clutched in his trembling hands and was scattering them, yet again, over his beloved boy. He barely glanced at Alyosha when he came in, and wouldn't look at anyone at all — not even at his deranged, weeping wife, ‘mamma,’ who kept trying to stand on her crippled legs to get a closer look at her dead son. Nina had been wheeled in her chair right up beside the coffin by the boys. She sat with her head pressed against it, weeping quietly too, no doubt. Snegiryov's face looked eager, yet bewildered and exasperated at once. There was something unhinged about his movements, about the words that kept bursting out of him. ‘Old man, dear old man!’ he exclaimed every minute, gazing at Ilusha. It had been his habit to call Ilusha ‘old man’ as a term of affection while he was alive.

“Father, give me a flower too — take that white one out of his hand and give it to me,” the deranged mother begged, whimpering. Whether it was because the little white rose in Ilusha's hand had caught her fancy, or because she wanted one from his own hand to keep in his memory, she stirred restlessly, reaching out her hands for the flower.
“I won't give it to anyone — I won't give you anything,” Snegiryov cried, coldly. “These are his flowers, not yours! Everything here is his, nothing is yours!”
“Father, give mother a flower!” said Nina, lifting a face wet with tears.

“I won't give anything away, and to her least of all! She never loved Ilusha. She took away his little cannon, and he gave it to her,” the captain broke into loud sobs at the memory of how Ilusha had given up his cannon to his mother. The poor, deranged woman was drowned in silent tears, her face hidden in her hands.
The boys, seeing that the father wouldn't leave the coffin and that it was time to carry it out, gathered in a tight circle around it and began to lift it.
“I don't want him buried in the churchyard,” Snegiryov suddenly wailed. “I'll bury him by the stone — by our stone! Ilusha told me to. I won't let him be carried out!”
He'd been saying for the past three days that he'd bury him by the stone, but Alyosha, Krassotkin, the landlady, her sister, and all the boys argued against it.

“What an idea — to bury him by some unholy stone, as if he'd hanged himself!” the old landlady said sternly. “There in the churchyard, the ground has been blessed. He'll be prayed for there. You can hear the singing in church, and the deacon reads so clearly, so distinctly, that it'll reach him every time, just as though it were being read right over his grave.”

At last the captain made a gesture of despair, as if to say, ‘Take him wherever you like.’ The boys lifted the coffin, but as they passed the mother, they paused for a moment and lowered it so she could say goodbye to Ilusha. But at the sight of that precious little face, which for the past three days she had only seen from a distance, she trembled all over, and her gray head began twitching spasmodically over the coffin.

“Mother, make the sign of the cross over him, give him your blessing, kiss him,” Nina cried to her. But her head kept twitching like some mechanical thing, and, her face twisted with bitter grief, she began, without a word, beating her breast with her fist. They carried the coffin past her. Nina pressed her lips to her brother's for the last time as they bore it by her. As Alyosha left the house, he asked the landlady to look after those left behind, but she cut him off before he'd finished.
“Of course I'll stay with them — we're Christians too.” The old woman wept as she said it.

They didn't have far to carry the coffin to the church — no more than three hundred paces. It was a still, clear day, with a light frost. The church bells were still ringing. Snegiryov hurried along behind the coffin, fussing, distracted, in his short old summer overcoat, bareheaded, his soft old wide-brimmed hat in his hand. He seemed caught up in a kind of bewildered anxiety. One minute he'd reach out to steady the head of the coffin, only getting in the bearers' way; the next he'd run alongside, trying to find some place for himself. A flower fell onto the snow, and he lunged to pick it up as though the whole world depended on that one lost flower.

“And the crust of bread — we've forgotten the crust!” he suddenly cried out in dismay. But the boys reminded him at once that he'd already taken the crust of bread, that it was in his pocket. He pulled it out instantly and was reassured.

“Ilusha told me to, Ilusha did,” he explained at once to Alyosha. “I was sitting with him one night, and he suddenly said to me: ‘Father, when they've filled in my grave, crumble some bread over it, so the sparrows will fly down — I'll hear them, and it'll cheer me up, not lying there all alone.’”
“That's a good thing to do,” said Alyosha. “We should bring some often.”
“Every day, every day!” the captain said quickly, seeming cheered by the thought.

They reached the church at last, and set the coffin down in the middle of it. The boys gathered around it and stood there, reverent, through the whole service. It was an old, rather poor church; many of the icons had no settings — but such churches are the best for praying in. During the mass, Snegiryov grew somewhat calmer, though every so often he had another outburst of that same unconscious, almost incoherent anxiety. At one point he went up to the coffin to straighten the cover or the wreath; when a candle fell out of its holder, he rushed to put it back and fumbled over it for an agonizingly long time, then settled down again and stood quietly by the coffin, his face full of blank unease and confusion. After the Epistle, he suddenly whispered to Alyosha, standing beside him, that the Epistle hadn't been read properly — but didn't explain what he meant. During the hymn ‘Like the Cherubim,’ he joined in the singing but didn't make it to the end. Falling to his knees, he pressed his forehead to the stone floor and stayed like that for a long time.

At last came the funeral service itself, and candles were handed out. The distracted father started fussing about again, but the touching, solemn funeral prayers moved and stirred his soul. He seemed to shrink in on himself all at once and broke into quick, short sobs, which he tried at first to stifle, but at last sobbed openly. When they began saying their farewells to the dead boy and closing the coffin, he flung his arms about, as though he wouldn't let them cover Ilusha, and began kissing his dead son's lips greedily, over and over. At last they managed to talk him down from the step, but he suddenly reached out and snatched a few flowers from the coffin. He looked at them, and some new idea seemed to dawn on him, so that for a moment he seemed to forget his grief entirely. Gradually he sank into a kind of brooding, and didn't resist when the coffin was lifted and carried to the grave. It was an expensive plot, close to the church, in the churchyard — Katerina Ivanovna had paid for it. After the customary rites, the gravediggers lowered the coffin. Snegiryov, flowers still in hand, bent so far over the open grave that the boys grabbed his coat in alarm and pulled him back. He didn't seem to fully grasp what was happening. When they began filling in the grave, he suddenly pointed anxiously at the falling earth and tried to say something, but no one could make out what he meant, and he broke off suddenly. Then they reminded him he had to crumble the bread, and he grew terribly excited, snatched up the loaf, began pulling it apart, and flung the pieces onto the grave.
“Come on, fly down, birds — fly down, sparrows!” he muttered anxiously.

One of the boys pointed out that it was awkward for him to crumble the bread with the flowers still in his hands, and suggested he give them to someone to hold for a while. But he wouldn't hear of it, and in fact seemed suddenly alarmed for his flowers, as though someone might try to take them away from him entirely. And after looking over the grave, satisfying himself, it seemed, that everything had been done and the bread duly crumbled, he suddenly, to everyone's surprise, turned around quite calmly and set off for home. But his steps grew quicker and quicker, until he was almost running. The boys and Alyosha kept pace with him.
“The flowers are for mamma, the flowers are for mamma! I was unkind to mamma,” he suddenly began exclaiming.

Someone called out for him to put his hat on, since it was cold. But he flung the hat down in the snow as if in anger, repeating, ‘I won't wear the hat, I won't wear the hat.’ Smurov picked it up and carried it after him. All the boys were crying, Kolya and the boy who'd discovered Troy crying hardest of all. Though Smurov, with the captain's hat in hand, was crying bitterly too, he still managed, as he ran, to snatch up a piece of red brick lying in the snow on the path and fling it at a flock of sparrows flying past. He missed, of course, and kept on crying as he ran. Halfway there, Snegiryov suddenly stopped short, stood frozen for half a minute as though struck by something, then turned back toward the church and ran for the abandoned grave. But the boys caught up with him at once and seized him on every side. He collapsed onto the snow as though knocked down, and, struggling, sobbing, wailing, began crying out, ‘Ilusha, old man, dear old man!’ Alyosha and Kolya tried to get him up, soothing him, coaxing him.
“Captain, that's enough — a brave man has to show some fortitude,” Kolya muttered.
“You'll ruin the flowers,” said Alyosha, “and mamma's waiting for them — she's sitting there crying because you wouldn't give her any before. Ilusha's little bed is still there—”

“Yes, yes, mamma!” Snegiryov suddenly remembered. “They'll take away the bed — they'll take it away,” he added, as though genuinely afraid it would happen. He jumped up and ran home again. But it wasn't far, and they all arrived together. Snegiryov threw open the door in a hurry and called to his wife, the very woman he'd quarreled with so cruelly not long before:

“Mamma, my poor crippled darling, Ilusha has sent you these flowers,” he cried, holding out to her a small bunch of flowers, frozen and crushed from his struggle in the snow. But at that same moment he caught sight, in the corner by the little bed, of Ilusha's little boots, which the landlady had set neatly side by side. At the sight of those old, patched, rust-colored, stiffened boots, he threw up his hands and rushed toward them, dropped to his knees, snatched up one boot, and, pressing his lips to it, began kissing it greedily, crying, ‘Ilusha, old man, dear old man, where are your little feet?’”

“Where have you taken him? Where have you taken him?” the poor demented woman cried, in a heartbreaking voice. Nina, too, broke into sobs. Kolya ran out of the room, and the other boys followed him. At last Alyosha went out as well.
“Let them cry,” he said to Kolya. “There's no use trying to comfort them right now. Let's wait a minute, then go back in.”

“No, it's no use — it's awful,” Kolya agreed. “Do you know, Karamazov,” he dropped his voice so no one else could hear, “I feel terribly sad, and if there were any way to bring him back, I'd give anything in the world to do it.”
“So would I,” said Alyosha.
“What do you think, Karamazov? Should we come back here tonight? He'll be drunk, you know.”

“Maybe he will. Let's come together, you and I — that will be enough, to spend an hour with them, with the mother and Nina. If we all come at once, we'll only remind them of everything all over again,” Alyosha suggested.
“The landlady's laying the table for them now — there'll be some kind of funeral dinner, the priest is coming. Shall we go back for it, Karamazov?”
“Of course,” said Alyosha.
“It's all so strange, Karamazov — such grief, and then pancakes right after it. It seems so unnatural, somehow, in our religion.”
“They're going to have salmon, too,” the boy who'd discovered Troy remarked, loudly.

“I'll ask you most earnestly, Kartashov, not to interrupt again with your idiotic remarks — especially when no one is talking to you, and no one particularly cares whether you exist or not!” Kolya snapped irritably. The boy flushed crimson but didn't dare answer back.
Meanwhile they'd been strolling slowly along the path, and suddenly Smurov exclaimed:
“There's Ilusha's stone — the one they wanted to bury him under.”

They all stopped by the big stone. Alyosha looked at it, and the whole scene Snegiryov had described to him that day rose up at once before his mind's eye — how Ilusha, weeping, clinging to his father, had cried, ‘Father, father, how he insulted you.’
A sudden impulse seemed to rise up in his soul. With a serious, earnest expression, he looked from one bright, pleasant face to another among Ilusha's schoolmates, and suddenly said to them:
“Boys, I'd like to say one thing to you, here, at this spot.”
The boys gathered around him and at once turned attentive, expectant eyes on him.

“Boys, we'll be parting soon. For a while I'll be staying with my two brothers — one of whom is bound for Siberia, and the other lying close to death. But soon I'll be leaving this town, perhaps for a long time, so we're going to part. Let's make a promise here, at Ilusha's stone, that we'll never forget Ilusha, or one another. And whatever happens to us later in life, even if we don't meet again for twenty years, let's always remember how we buried this poor boy — the one we once threw stones at, do you remember, by the bridge? — and how we all grew so fond of him afterward. He was a fine boy — kindhearted, brave — he cared about his father's honor, resented the cruel insult done to him, and stood up for him. And so, first of all, let's remember him, boys, for the rest of our lives. And even if we get caught up in the most important things in the world, even if we rise to great honor or fall into great misfortune — let's still remember how good it was, once, here, when we were all together, bound by a good, kind feeling that made us, for as long as we loved that poor boy, better people than we are, perhaps, the rest of the time. My little doves — let me call you that, because right now, looking at your good, dear faces, you remind me so much of them, those pretty blue birds. My dear children, maybe you won't understand what I'm telling you, because I often speak rather unclearly, but you'll remember it all the same, and you'll agree with me someday. You should know that there's nothing higher, nothing stronger, nothing healthier or more useful for life afterward than some good memory — especially a memory from childhood, from home. People talk to you endlessly about your education, but some good, sacred memory, kept safe from childhood, may be the best education of all. If a man carries many such memories with him into life, he's safe to the end of his days — and even if a person has only one good memory left in his heart, that alone might someday be enough to save him. Perhaps we'll even grow wicked as we get older, unable to resist some bad action, laughing at people's tears, at those who say, as Kolya just said, ‘I want to suffer for all mankind’ — we might even sneer spitefully at people like that. But however wicked we may become — God forbid — still, when we remember how we buried Ilusha, how we loved him in his last days, and how we've been talking together like friends, right here, at this stone — even the cruelest, most mocking among us, if that's what we become, won't dare, inside himself, to laugh at having been kind and good in this moment! What's more — perhaps that one memory alone will keep him from some great evil, and he'll stop and say to himself, ‘Yes, I was good and brave and honest once.’ Let him laugh to himself if he wants — that's no matter; people often laugh at what's good and kind. That's only thoughtlessness. But I promise you, boys, that even as he laughs, he'll say at once, in his heart, ‘No — I'm wrong to laugh, because that's nothing to laugh at.’”
“That will be so — I understand you, Karamazov!” Kolya cried, his eyes shining.
The boys were stirred, and they wanted to say something too, but held themselves back, watching the speaker with rapt, emotional attention.

“I'm saying this in case we turn out bad,” Alyosha went on, “but there's no reason we should turn out bad, is there, boys? Let's be, first and above all, kind — then honest — and then let's never forget each other! I say it again. I give you my word, for my part, that I'll never forget a single one of you. Every face looking at me right now, I'll remember, even thirty years from now. Just a moment ago, Kolya told Kartashov that we didn't care whether he existed or not. But I can't forget that Kartashov exists, and that he isn't blushing now, the way he did when he discovered who founded Troy, but is looking at me with his cheerful, kind, dear little eyes. Boys, my dear boys, let's all be generous and brave, like Ilusha, clever and brave and generous like Kolya (though he'll be far cleverer still once he's grown), and let's all be as modest, as clever, as sweet as Kartashov. But why am I singling out just those two? All of you are dear to me, boys, from this day on — I've kept a place in my heart for every one of you, and I ask you to keep a place in your hearts for me too! Well then — who was it who brought us together in this good, kind feeling, which we'll remember, and mean to remember, our whole lives long? Who, if not Ilusha — the good boy, the dear boy, precious to us forever! Let's never forget him. May his memory live forever in our hearts, from this moment on!”
“Yes, yes, forever, forever!” the boys cried out, in ringing voices, their faces softened.
“Let's remember his face, and his clothes, and his poor little boots, his coffin, and his unhappy, sinful father, and how bravely he stood up for him, alone, against the whole school.”
“We will remember, we will remember,” the boys cried. “He was brave, he was good!”
“Ah, how I loved him!” Kolya exclaimed.
“Ah, children, ah, dear friends — don't be afraid of life! How good life is, when you do something good and just!”
“Yes, yes,” the boys repeated, enthusiastically.
“Karamazov, we love you!” a voice — Kartashov's, probably — cried out impulsively.
“We love you, we love you!” they all took it up. Tears stood in many of their eyes.
“Hurrah for Karamazov!” Kolya shouted, in an ecstasy.
“And may the dead boy's memory live forever!” Alyosha added again, with feeling.
“Forever!” the boys chimed in again.
“Karamazov,” Kolya cried, “can it really be true, what religion teaches us — that we'll all rise again from the dead, and live, and see each other again — everyone, Ilusha too?”
“Certainly we'll all rise again, certainly we'll see each other again, and tell each other, with joy and gladness, everything that's happened!” Alyosha answered, half laughing, half in earnest.
“Ah, how wonderful that will be!” burst from Kolya.

“Well, now let's finish talking and go to his funeral dinner. Don't mind us eating pancakes — it's a very old custom, and there's something good in that!” Alyosha laughed. “Come, let's go! And now, we go hand in hand.”
“And always like this, hand in hand, our whole lives long! Hurrah for Karamazov!” Kolya cried once more, rapturously, and once again the boys took up his cry: ‘Hurrah for Karamazov!’
THE END
FOOTNOTES
[1] In Russian, “silen.”
[2] A proverbial saying in Russia.
[3] Grushenka.
[4] That is, a setter dog.
[5] This likely refers to the Decembrist plot against the Tsar in December 1825, in which some of the most distinguished men in Russia were implicated. — Translator's note.

[6] When a monk's body is carried from his cell to the church, and from the church to the graveyard, the hymn “What earthly joy...” is sung. If the deceased was also a priest, the hymn “Our Helper and Defender” is sung instead.
[7] That is, a chime of bells.
[8] Literally: “Did they make a long nose at you?” — a Russian proverbial expression for failure.
[9] Gogol is meant.
